chapter: Later career and The Benny Goodman Story
title: Recap of Goodman days, 1936-45
summary: Wilson summarizes the trio, leaving in 1939, the Cafe Society years, and rejoining Goodman in 1944-45 for Seven Lively Arts and then the sextet.

story.theme_name: Working for Benny Goodman: the leader and his bands
story.community_name: Working for Benny Goodman: the perfectionist bandleader

blocks.x: I think we could continue now -- this is January 3rd and we can just continue on. I'd like to ask you something about -- some of the Goodman days, we talked about you being in the band, and we spoke about the band and
you joining them and playing in Chicago, but you haven't spoken really in depth about it, so tell me something about how you got along with Benny and how the band worked out.
Well, I'm sure we covered the formation of the Goodman trio.
Yes, we did.

The house party at Mildred Bailey's house and Red Norvo and Mildred Bailey and John Hammond organizing the session. Then later Goodman became a bandleader and kept a steady group together on the road and hired me to come along with the trio along with Gene Krupa and later on, a quartet with Lionel Hampton.
And I think we finished Colorado Springs -- we were talking about the Seven Lively Arts show, which I did, with Bert Lahr.
Yes, we were.

Let's see, I had left Goodman, of course, in '39 and formed my own big band for a year and a half and cut down to the small six-piece group, or seven-piece group to play the Cafe Society uptown and downtown all during the Second World War, up until 1945 where I rejoined Benny to play in the quintet in the Seven Lively Arts, the quintet of Red Norvo, Morty Feld, Sid Weiss on bass, Morty Feld on drums, Red Norvo and Goodman and myself.
Now that might be where we left off.
I think so.
And that would have been ...
What year was that, did you say?
That would be 1944.
Uh huh.

And after that show, I stayed on with Goodman for quite a while, maybe another 6 or 8 months or so, I guess, because he had a big band and a small band; we played some dates on the road and in the New England area, and then for quite a long run at the 400 Restaurant, I believe it would be, on Fifth Avenue in those days, and he still had a sextet then with Slim Stewart on bass and Mike Bryan on the guitar, and Morey Feld still on drums and Red Norvo and myself. In that group, we recorded some Columbia sextet records -- I guess I'm getting up to around 1945, now, right after the war.
Now wait, I'm getting a little confused. Now is this after Lionel Hampton had been there?
Oh, Lionel had his own band at this time.
Oh, I see.
Yes, Lionel went on his own back in, I think around '40 or 41. I went on my own in '39.
Yeah, right.
And then back with Goodman in '44 for the Seven Lively Arts Show, and this was '45, this period, still back after the show with the organization, and the new

sextet, as I said, was Slam and Mike Bryan, Red Norvo and some of the records that were recorded were with me on piano and somewhere - so there were the 78's, they still didn't have the LP's, it was 78's with some of the sides done by Mel Powell on piano. But otherwise, the personnel were exactly the same.
I see.
I'm trying to think of the young lady's name who sang on some of those -- but I can't think of it right now.
It wasn't Helen ...

No. She was on television, on the old Broadway Open House show with Jerry Lester and Dagmar, do you remember that show? The accordion player was the band leader. The young lady who sang -- let me pause for a minute and shut this off while I think of it.
